periods.activity_title: Into the Story: Abbakka's World and First Stand

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us read — pre-reading riddle (p.206): solve riddle, share women-warrior names.

time_bands.activity: Open with the pre-reading riddle from "Let us read" (p.206) — read it aloud together and invite quick volunteer answers. Briefly collect names of other women warriors students already know, accepting one or two contributions before moving on.

Teacher reads the narrative of Rani Abbakka (pp.206–213) aloud at an unhurried pace while students follow in their books. Pause briefly at key plot turns — Abbakka refusing tribute, rallying allies, forging the Arabian trade route — to let students absorb the scene.

Brief whole-class discussion: what was Abbakka's first act of defiance, and why did her husband consider it rash? Take three or four student responses and draw out the idea of sovereignty before closing the unit.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit opens the narrative; the pre-reading riddle warms students up to Abbakka's world before they hear her story. A common pitfall here is rushing the read-aloud — the textbook text appears in illustrated format, so read slowly and describe key images aloud where the printed text is thin. Students unfamiliar with 16th-century coastal Karnataka may need a one-sentence geographical note on Ullal's position as a trading port.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.213–214): word-meaning match and cause-and-effect table.
Let us think and reflect (p.214–215): tribute meaning, sovereignty fill-in, true/false.

homework.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.215): answer the four extended-response questions on Abbakka's inspiration.

time_bands.activity: Recall the story read in the previous unit by asking students: what did Abbakka do after refusing tribute? Accept two quick responses to re-anchor the narrative before moving to exercises.

Work through "Let us discuss" (p.213–214) — students attempt the word-meaning matching pairs individually, then pairs compare answers. Confirm the full match list together, pausing on 'vassal', 'sovereign country', and 'dauntless' to unpack meaning in context.

Move to the cause-and-effect table (p.214): teacher models the first completed row, then students fill in the remaining blanks in pairs. Discuss each cause–effect chain as a class, emphasising how Abbakka's decisions triggered Portuguese escalation.

From "Let us think and reflect" (p.214–215), handle the three shorter items together — the meaning of 'tribute', the sovereignty fill-in, and the true/false statement. The extended-response questions are set as a written homework task.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read Abbakka's resistance aloud, students are now ready to examine its logic through cause and effect. A common pitfall is treating the matching exercise as a vocabulary test in isolation — connect each word back to a moment in the narrative (e.g., 'resolve' — where did Abbakka show resolve?). The extended-response questions on inspiration and the people's mindset require inference and personal response, which is why they move to homework where students can write without time pressure.

periods.activity_title: Listening to Rani Gaidinliu; Pronouncing Abbakka's Vocabulary

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us listen (p.220): bio-table fill-in for Rani Gaidinliu from teacher talk.
Let us speak (p.221): paired pronunciation and syllable-stress practice of seven words.

time_bands.activity: Distribute or display the bio-table for Rani Gaidinliu (p.220) and read the column headers aloud together. Tell students they will fill in the blanks as they listen — they should not write anything yet.

Read the teacher's talk on Rani Gaidinliu (p.224) aloud at a clear, steady pace — this is the listening passage. Students fill in their bio-table as they listen. After the first reading, allow a brief pause for students to check their entries, then read the passage once more.

Verify the bio-table together as a class — teacher reads each field and cold-calls students for their answer. Correct any mishearing and draw a brief comparison between Gaidinliu's story and Abbakka's: both resisted colonial rule and were captured but unbroken.

Shift to "Let us speak" (p.221): teacher models the pronunciation of each of the seven words (vassal, successor, rash, league, wrath, seize, resolve), noting syllable count and stress. Students then practise in pairs, taking turns saying each word while their partner listens and gives a thumbs-up or correction.

periods.teacher_notes: Having absorbed Abbakka's story and vocabulary through reading, students now encounter a second braveheart through listening — the parallel reinforces the chapter's theme of women's resistance to colonial power. A common pitfall in the bio-table exercise is students writing while still trying to listen; a brief preview of the headers before the reading gives them a mental framework so they can focus on listening first. For the pronunciation task, 'wrath' (silent w) and 'seize' (not 'size') are the two words most likely to cause confusion — model these with a minimal-pair contrast.

periods.activity_title: Writing a Conversation: Women and India's Identity

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write (p.221): draft a Pratap–Tarana conversation on women's role in India's identity.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the writing task from "Let us write" (p.221): display the opening lines for Pratap and Tarana and read them aloud. Facilitate a brief class brainstorm — what contributions by women (historical and contemporary) could the two characters discuss? List five or six ideas on the board.

Model the first two exchanges of the conversation on the board, thinking aloud about how to make each speaker's voice distinct, how to reference a specific woman's achievement, and how to keep the exchange flowing naturally.

Students write their conversation independently — six to eight sentences for each speaker, building on the board model and the brainstormed ideas. Teacher circulates, prompting students who are stuck with questions like 'Which woman did you just study this term?' or 'What did Abbakka achieve that Pratap might admire?'

Two or three pairs read their conversations aloud to the class. After each reading, invite one brief peer comment: 'What was the most convincing point Pratap or Tarana made?' Close with a reminder that a strong conversation names specific achievements, not just general praise.

periods.teacher_notes: Having studied both Abbakka and Gaidinliu through reading and listening, students have fresh, concrete material to draw on for this conversation task. A common pitfall is students writing vague sentiments ('women are great') rather than grounding their dialogue in specific examples — the board brainstorm and the circulating prompts are designed to keep the writing anchored. The guided-writing scaffold (opening lines already provided) reduces the blank-page problem; the teacher's job is to keep students moving from general admiration to specific, reasoned argument.
materials: Board or display surface for brainstorm and model

periods.activity_title: Spelling Rules, Silent Letters, Laugh Expressions, and Reported Speech

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.215): 'ie/ei' spelling rule — fill in ten blanks.
Let us learn (p.219): direct-to-indirect speech — rewrite six sentences.

homework.task_brief: Let us learn (p.216): find meanings of four 'laugh' expressions and write original sentences.

time_bands.activity: Open with the 'i before e except after c' rule from "Let us learn" (p.215), linking it to 'seize' and 'sovereign' from Abbakka's story. Students complete the ten ie/ei blanks individually, then swap books with a partner for peer correction.

Briefly surface the silent-letter idea using 'wrath' (silent w) alongside the examples in "Let us learn" (p.216) — campaign, knowledge, pneumonia, honour, calm. Invite students to call out one or two more words they know; confirm or gently correct, then move on rather than exhausting the list.

Introduce direct and indirect speech (p.219): teacher writes one direct-speech sentence on the board and models the transformation step by step — tense back-shift, pronoun change, removal of quotation marks. Students then rewrite the six given sentences in pairs, checking each other's tense and pronoun changes.

Review two of the reported-speech answers together as a class to address recurring errors. Set the 'laugh' expressions task (p.216) as homework and explain clearly what is expected: find the meaning of each expression using the dictionary page provided, then write one original sentence per expression.

periods.teacher_notes: The ie/ei rule and the reported-speech conversion are the two highest-demand items in the vocabulary and grammar work for this section; handling both in class ensures teacher support is available for the tricky pronoun shifts and tense back-shifts in indirect speech. A common pitfall is students applying the 'i before e except after c' rule mechanically without recognising exceptions such as 'seize' and 'sovereign', which appear in the very text they have read — draw attention to these counter-examples explicitly. The 'laugh' expressions task is self-contained enough for independent homework use.

periods.activity_title: Chapter Synthesis: Brave Women Across Time — Research, Present, Reflect

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us explore (p.222): group research and in-class presentation on one brave woman.

time_bands.activity: Open with a whole-class reflection: across Abbakka and Gaidinliu, what common threads of courage and resistance stand out? Accept three or four responses to create a shared frame before groups begin their own research.

Groups of five choose one woman from "Let us explore" (p.222) — Rani Chennamma, Rani Durgavati, Ahilyabai Holkar, Jhalkari Bai, Captain Lakshmi Sahgal, Kanaklata Barua, Kalpana Chawla, or another. Using their textbooks and any reference material available in class, groups plan their presentation across five headings: Childhood, Training/Education, Achievements, Contributions, and What we learnt from her.

Each group delivers a brief oral presentation (one to two minutes each). Listeners note one fact they did not know; the teacher asks one connecting question per group — linking the presented woman's story back to Abbakka's themes of sovereignty, courage, or resistance to power.

Close with a whole-chapter synthesis: teacher draws together the common thread — bravehearted resistance to oppression, across centuries and contexts — and invites one student per group to name the single most striking parallel between their chosen woman and Rani Abbakka.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit draws the chapter together by moving from Abbakka's specific story to a broader pattern of women's courage in Indian history, making the chapter's theme transferable. A common pitfall is groups spending all their time on biography and neglecting the 'what we learnt' heading — prompt each group to include at least one sentence on personal learning before they present. Where reference materials are limited, encourage groups to draw on what the textbook itself says about the chapter's women rather than guessing.
materials: Any available reference books or library resources

items.source_lo: Student identifies and interprets explicit and implicit meanings in a historical narrative using reading for comprehension as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Abbakka's refusal of tribute, cause-and-effect chains, sovereignty, 'dauntless' and 'resolve' vocabulary, extract analysis.
items.item_stem:
Read the following statements about Rani Abbakka's actions in the narrative and identify whether each statement is true or false.
1. Abbakka agreed to pay tribute to the Portuguese because she feared their military strength.
2. Abbakka forged a trading alliance with Arabia to defy the Portuguese economic blockade.
3. Abbakka personally led a midnight counter-attack and entered the Portuguese fort.
4. Abbakka's husband Veera Narsimha supported her decision to refuse tribute from the very beginning.

options.text: Abbakka agreed to pay tribute to the Portuguese because she feared their military strength.
Abbakka forged a trading alliance with Arabia to defy the Portuguese economic blockade.
Abbakka personally led a midnight counter-attack and entered the Portuguese fort.
Abbakka's husband Veera Narsimha supported her decision to refuse tribute from the very beginning.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer:
1. False — Abbakka refused tribute outright, declaring Ullal a sovereign country that owed Portugal nothing.
2. True — She established a profitable trading relationship with Arabia directly to counter the Portuguese blockade.
3. True — She led a midnight raid, entered the Portuguese fort, and killed their commander.
4. False — Veera Narsimha called her decision rash and ordered soldiers to stop her.

items.source_lo: Student identifies and interprets explicit and implicit meanings in a historical narrative using reading for comprehension as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Abbakka's refusal of tribute, cause-and-effect chains, sovereignty, 'dauntless' and 'resolve' vocabulary, extract analysis.
items.item_stem: In the narrative, when Abbakka's estranged husband Veera Narsimha collaborated with the Portuguese, her forces were weakened — yet she continued to resist until she was captured. What does this sequence of events reveal about the nature of Abbakka's resolve? Support your answer with at least two specific details from the story.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Abbakka's resolve is shown to be unconditional — it did not depend on the loyalty of those around her. Even when betrayed from within and militarily weakened, she kept fighting, demonstrating that her commitment to Ullal's sovereignty came from personal conviction rather than favourable circumstances.

items.source_context: Rani Gaidinliu: Naga leader, Heraka movement, arrest at 16, life imprisonment, 'Rani' title, Padma Bhushan, Silchar statue.
items.item_stem: Your teacher will read the biographical account of Rani Gaidinliu. Listen carefully and complete the table below.
items.visual_stimulus:
Field|Answer
Year Gaidinliu was born|__________
Name of the movement she joined in 1927|__________
Age at which she was arrested|__________
Title given to her by the then Prime Minister|__________
Award received in 1982|__________

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. 1915. 2. The Heraka movement. 3. 16 (sixteen). 4. 'Rani' (and 'Daughter of the Hills'). 5. Padma Bhushan.

items.source_lo: Student extracts and records specific factual information from a listened-to biographical account using listening for information as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Rani Gaidinliu: Naga leader, Heraka movement, arrest at 16, life imprisonment, 'Rani' title, Padma Bhushan, Silchar statue.
items.item_stem: Based on the biographical account of Rani Gaidinliu, explain in two to three sentences why the title 'Daughter of the Hills' is particularly appropriate for her. Use at least two specific facts from the account in your answer.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Gaidinliu was born in the hill district of Tamenglong in Manipur and spent her life working for the Naga people of the northeastern hill regions. She led an armed uprising across Manipur, Nagaland, and Assam — all hill territories — and after her release in 1947 continued to serve her hill community, making 'Daughter of the Hills' a precise reflection of both her origins and her lifelong work.

items.source_context: Syllable stress and phonetic features of vassal, successor, rash, league, wrath, seize, resolve from the narrative.
items.item_stem: Say each of the following words from the story of Rani Abbakka aloud. Your teacher will listen for the correct number of syllables and the correct syllable receiving stress. Words: vassal, successor, resolve.

expected_elements: Pronounces 'vassal' as two syllables with stress on first syllable.
Pronounces 'successor' as three syllables with stress on second syllable.
Pronounces 'resolve' as two syllables with the /z/ sound for the medial 's'.
Speaks clearly at a pace that allows syllable boundaries to be heard.

items.item_stem: Choose any two of the following words from the narrative — wrath, seize, league, rash — and use each in a spoken sentence about Rani Abbakka's story. Your teacher will listen for accurate pronunciation of the word and a sentence that makes sense in the context of the narrative.

expected_elements: Pronounces both chosen words accurately, including silent letters where applicable.
Sentence is meaningfully connected to an event in Abbakka's story.
Word is used with its correct meaning in the sentence.
Speaks at a natural pace with clear articulation of the chosen word.

items.item_stem: Write a short conversation of four exchanges (two lines for each speaker) between two students discussing one specific achievement of Rani Abbakka that they find most inspiring. Begin with: 'Arjun: I think the most remarkable thing about Rani Abbakka was...' Each speaker must give a reason for their view.

expected_elements: Each speaker names a specific achievement from the narrative.
Each speaker gives at least one reason supporting their view.
Dialogue moves forward — second speaker responds to first.
Writing uses correct dialogue punctuation and paragraph formatting.

items.source_context: Conversation between Pratap and Tarana on women's role in shaping India's identity as a strong nation.
items.item_stem: Write a conversation of six to eight exchanges between two students — one who believes that the most important quality a leader like Abbakka had was courage, and the other who believes it was strategic thinking (such as forging trade alliances or planning the midnight counter-attack). Each speaker should support their position with details from the narrative and acknowledge the other's point at least once.

expected_elements: Both positions are supported with specific details from the narrative.
At least one speaker acknowledges or responds to the other's argument.
Conversation sustains a coherent line of reasoning across exchanges.
Writing uses correct dialogue formatting and appropriate register.

items.item_stem: Complete the table below. Each word in Column A is taken from or related to the story of Rani Abbakka. Choose the correctly spelled form of the missing letters from the pair given in brackets and write it in Column B.
items.visual_stimulus:
Word (with gap)|Missing letters (choose one)|Correct spelling
s___ze (from Abbakka's story: 'to take hold of suddenly')|(ie / ei)|__________
bel___ve (as in 'Abbakka believed in Ullal's sovereignty')|(ie / ei)|__________
sh___ld (a warrior's protective gear)|(ie / ei)|__________
perc___ve (to understand or notice)|(ie / ei)|__________
ch___f (a leader or head of a group)|(ie / ei)|__________

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. seize — ei. 2. believe — ie. 3. shield — ie. 4. perceive — ei. 5. chief — ie.

items.item_stem:
The sentences below are based on events in the story of Rani Abbakka. Rewrite each sentence in indirect speech, making all necessary changes to tense, pronouns, and reporting expressions.
1. Abbakka declared, 'We are a sovereign country and we owe nothing to Portugal.'
2. The Portuguese envoy warned her, 'Our Governor will not tolerate this refusal.'

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. Abbakka declared that they were a sovereign country and they owed nothing to Portugal. 2. The Portuguese envoy warned her that their Governor would not tolerate that refusal.

items.item_stem: In groups of four or five, research one brave Indian woman of your choice — for example, Rani Durgavati, Ahilyabai Holkar, Jhalkari Bai, Captain Lakshmi Sahgal, or Kanaklata Barua — and prepare a short written profile covering the following headings: (1) Childhood, (2) Training or Education, (3) Achievements, (4) Contributions to society or the nation. Present your profile to the class.

expected_elements: Profile covers all four required headings with factual content.
Achievements and contributions are distinct and specific, not generic.
Presentation is organised and delivered clearly to the class.
Group divides the headings among members for equitable contribution.

items.item_stem: After presenting your group's research, write a reflective paragraph (eight to ten sentences) comparing your chosen woman with Rani Abbakka. In your paragraph, identify at least two qualities or circumstances that the two women share, and explain what lesson you personally draw from both their lives.

expected_elements: Names at least two specific shared qualities or circumstances with textual evidence.
Comparison is analytical, not merely listing facts side by side.
Personal learning is expressed as a genuine reflection, not a cliché.
Writing is coherent across eight to ten sentences with appropriate register.
